2. In writ Petition No.4206 of 2009 initiation of Tejgaon PS Case No. 53 dated 19-3-2009 under sections 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, sections 420/409/109 of the Penal pending before the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Dhaka has been challenged by the petitioners. 

 3. Similarly in Writ petition No. 5067 of 2009, Writ petition No. 4202 of 2009 and Writ petition No. 4207 of 2009 petitioners have challenged initiation of Tejgaon Police Station Case No.53 dated 19-3-2009, Tejgaon Police Station Case No.54 dated 19-3-2009 and Tejgaon Police Station Case No.55 dated 19-3-2009 respectively all under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 read with sections 420/409/109 of the Penal Code under different grounds. 

 4. Facts are almost similar in all the petitions and in all these cases as we have found that right after lodging of the FIR the petitioners moved this Division under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the Rules. 

 6. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan and Mr. AKM Fazlul Hoque, the learned counsels appearing on behalf of the Anti-Corruption Commission, on the other hand, oppose all the Rules. Mr. AKM Fazlul Hoque, the learned counsel filed affidavit in oppositions in writ petition Nos, 4206, 5067 and 4207 of 2009 and submits that leaving aside all the points those are settled by the Appellate Division and this Division, the writ petitions are no maintainable as being pre-mature. In paragraph 24 of the affidavit in opposition tiled in writ petition No. 4206 of 2009 it has been categorically stated that the petitioners are fugitive from justice or law and have no right to seek aid or assistance of any Court and the Court will not pass any order in their aid. This view finds support in the decisions reported in Anti-Corruption Com- mission vs Md Hossain 61 DLR (AD) 17. Anti-Corruption Commission vs Dr HBM Alamgir 15 BLC (AD) 44 and Anti-Corruption Commission vs ATM Nazimullah Chowdhury 62 DLR (AD) 225. It is to be mentioned that the initiation of the cases against the petitioners alleging offences under different sections of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 and the Penal Code will be followed by subsequent procedure of law governing the same. 

 7. Mr. Md Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned counsel for the respondent in Writ petition No. 4202 of 2009 submits that right after lodging of the FIR when the investigation had just started the petitioner brought this writ petition which is also not tenable under law since no proceeding as such was pending before any competent Court of jurisdiction and tor this reason interference by this Division at an initial stage of investigation cannot be supported under law. In this regard the decision of Abdul Hoque vs the State reported in 60 DLR (AD) 1 has been relied upon wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division unanimously held that before taking of cognizance of a case by a competent Court for tribunal a proceeding cannot be said to be pending and accordingly, a proceeding cannot be quashed unless cognizance in respect thereof has been taken and process issued. 

 8. We have heard the learned counsels for the petitioners and the respondents and considered their submissions. We have also gone through the petitions and the different Annexure and the supplementary affidavits carefully. Since the decision of our apex Court clearly spelt out the provision of section 32 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act in this context holding no sanction is required before filling a case under the act and also on the point that a case cannot be quashed unless cognizance has been taken by the Court having jurisdiction we are of the view that both the points apply adversely in the instant writ petitions. 

 9. It has been argued that in violation of section 32(1)(2) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 the FIR was lodged against the petitioner since no sanction was obtained by the Commission as required under that said provision. We hold that this question has been set at rest which is no longer a resintegra. No sanction is required for lodging any FIR in contemplation with section 32(1)(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act 2004 un-amended or amended. This view reached in its finality in a very recent decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Anti-Corruption Commission vs Dr. Mohiuddin Khan Alamgir reported in 62 DLR (AD) 290 wherein his Lordship Mr. Justice ABM Khairul Hoque while construing this point observed: - 

 "The High-Court Division, however, misinterpreted Section 32 of the Act, the original as well as the amended one, in holding that a sanction by the Commission is required before lodging an FIR. The High Court Division further misconceived the amended section 32 and wrongly held that a further sanction is required to take cognizance Of the offence by the Court in spite of the sanction given earlier under Sub-section (2) of Section 32 of the Act. But as a matter of fact no sanction is required to file a complaint and the unamended as well as the amended section 32 requires only one sanction from the Commission. 

 The second argument of the Learned Counsel for the respondent Mr. Khurshid Alam Khan that right after lodging of the FIR when the investigation had just started the petitioner brought this writ petition for which the same is not tenable under law since no proceeding as such was pending before any competent court of jurisdiction also merits substance. In this regard the decision of Abdul Hoque vs the State 60 DLR (AD) 1 as referred to above can profitable be cited wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division after discussing pertinent potion of the reported cases of Bangladesh vs Tan Khong Hock 31 DLR (AD) 69. Syed Mohammad Hashem alias Hashim vs State 48 DLR (AD) 87 and N Mahmud vs N Ahmed 36 DLR (AD) 14 unanimously held: All the cases seeking quashing of the proceedings were preferred before taking of cognizance of the offence by the senior Metropolitan Special Judge 	Accordingly, before taking of cognizance of a case by competent court or tribunal a proceeding cannot be said to be pending. And accordingly a proceeding cannot be quashed unless cognizance in respect thereof has been taken process issued and so the instant criminal miscellaneous cases preferred under section 561A the Code of Criminal Procedure are guite premature and so the High Court Division should not enter into the first information report and the charge sheet in order to appreciate whether the facts alleged therein constitute any offence or not. 

 10. The process that has to be followed after lodging of the FIR cannot be throttled or stifled at an initial stage of the case. The petitioners however will have ample opportunity to argue their cases before the appropriate forum in due course. Therefore, at this moment we are not going to digress into any point touching upon the merit of the respective cases against the petitioners, 

 11. Moreover, from the perusal of the writ petition No. 4202 of 2009 in paragraph No. 19 as well as the prayer 'd' it appears that the writ petitioners without surrendering before any Court of law filed the writ petition and obtained rule and stay challenging the lodging of Tejgaon PS Case No. 54 dated 19-03-09 under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sections 420/409/109 of the Penal Code, pending before the Court. of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. 

 12. The principle of criminal jurisprudence is that a person concerned should submit to the process of justice before he can. claim right of audience provided in law as well as the judicial convention, which is very much effective in the Court of law as the age-old maxim goes that a person who seeks justice from the Court of the law must come before the Court to agitate his grievance and must surrender first to the process of justice, otherwise, he remains to be fugitive from justice and cannot seek aid of assistance of the process of justice in .order to claim right of audience against the process of the Court issued against him. When an FIR lodged he immediately becomes wanted by the Court in order to give effect to the order of the Court. His appearance is ensured by means of a warrant if necessary. If he does not surrender to the process nor his arrest is secured, then dispensation of justice is defeated. He remains a fugitive from justice. In the case Chand Shah vs Crown reported in 8 DLR (FC) 24 it has been held that it was an essential condition of an administration of justice in a case affecting an individual or individuals, that the persons concerned should submit to the process of justice. It has been further held in the Chand Shah's case that the Attorney-General who appeared to secure the interference of the Court on behalf of fugitives, without ensuing that such persons conform to the judicial orders applicable to them, was not acting in accordance with his proper duty to acting furtherance of justice. 

 14. In a recent decision our Appellate Division held in the case of State vs Zakaria Pintu alias Md Zakaria Pintu reported in 18 BLT (AD) (2010) 491 = 62 DLR (AD) 420 that a bail although may often be a right to an accused but sometimes it is imperative on the part of the Court to refuse if there is serious allegations against him, like murder, rape, violence etc., because the Court just always keep in mind that justice must ultimately be done by ensuring punishment upon the offender otherwise, the offenders will get upper hand and, the sober of section of the society will suffer, which will destroy the fabrics. After all, it is the first and foremost duty of the State to bring the offender to book in order to ensure justice in the society. In the said reported case in paragraph 16 it has been observed: 

 15. In the instant case the petitioners were fugitive from justice when moved the writ petition and obtained the Rule and stay. In view of the above, at the time of 'motion' hearing this Division wrongly entertained the writ petition and stayed the investigation against the writ petitioners.
